Eminent

EM-uh-nunt · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Eminent means widely recognized as outstanding, distinguished, and highly respected within a particular field.

The conference had drawn the most eminent geologists in the world, scholars whose names filled the very textbooks the students had studied all year.

Worked Example

The eminent judge's landmark rulings on privacy law are still dissected line by line in first-year classrooms at every law school in the country.

Notice why eminent is the right word here: the judge is not merely known, she is widely recognized as outstanding and distinguished within her field, and that recognition was earned through the quality of her legal work. That is the heart of eminent: prominence built on genuine expertise and the respect of one's peers. Do not confuse it with the look-alike imminent, which sounds similar but means about to happen (an imminent storm, an imminent deadline) and has nothing to do with reputation. Also keep eminent distinct from a looser word like famous: a reality-TV star can be famous for pure spectacle, but eminent reserves its praise for people whose standing rests on achievement and mastery, not just visibility.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

distinguished: The closest everyday match — marked out as excellent by a record of achievement, slightly plainer than eminent's sense of standing at the very top of a field.

renowned: Emphasizes how far one's fame has spread; eminent leans more on the quality and authority behind the reputation than on how far the name has traveled.

esteemed: Highlights the respect and high regard others hold for the person, whereas eminent foregrounds the person's own demonstrated superiority.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

obscure: Unknown and unnoticed, with no recognized standing in any field — the direct opposite of earned, widely acknowledged distinction.

undistinguished: Having no record of special achievement — competent perhaps, but with nothing that lifts the person above the ordinary ranks of the field.

Where it sits · how widely the reputation reaches — competent → respected → eminent

competent vs. eminent: A competent researcher meets the field's standard; an eminent one has helped define it, standing among the handful of names everyone in the discipline knows.

respected vs. eminent: A respected colleague earns admiration inside her own department, but an eminent scholar's authority is acknowledged across the entire field.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-

Prefix — e-: out, out of (a form of Latin ex-)

Root — -min-

Root — -min-: to project, jut out (Latin minere, related to mons, "mountain")

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: in a state of; forms adjectives from verbs

Put it together

Put it together: Latin eminere meant "to stand out, jut out" — e- ("out") plus minere ("to project," a root related to mons, "mountain"). The adjective suffix -ent describes something in that state. So an eminent person literally "juts out" above the surrounding landscape of a profession, the way a peak rises above foothills. The same jutting root builds prominent ("jutting forward") and promontory (a headland projecting into the sea). One caution: this min- means "project," not "small" — minimal and minute come from a completely different root.

Use the root in a new word: promontory

Use the root in a new word: promontory: The lighthouse stood on a rocky promontory that jutted out over the sea — the same Latin root, minere, "to project."

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / respectful

Eminent is a formal word of praise. Reserve it for people of serious, established standing in a profession or field — it would sound oddly grand applied to a friend or to someone merely popular.
